papers.record_title: The Coralia Sequence: A Unique Finite Integer Set Under Fibonacci-Lucas Terminal Constraints
papers.pdf_title: The Coralia Sequence: A Unique Finite Integer Set Under Fibonacci-Lucas Terminal Constraints
papers.abstract_html_from_record: We introduce the Coralia Sequence C = {0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 9, 12, 15, 23, 30, 35}, a 12-element integer set characterized by nine axioms (C1–C9). The sequence is generated by four arithmetic zones with non-decreasing initial gaps, followed by a strictly descending terminal gap triple drawn from the Fibonacci and Lucas numbers. We prove that C is the unique 12-element completion of a 10-element seed satisfying the stated axioms. In particular, the terminal gap triple (8, 7, 5) = (F_6, L_4, F_5) is shown to be the unique strictly descending triple from the Fibonacci–Lucas set whose elements sum to 20 and are all at least 5. Exhaustive verification code supporting the uniqueness result is publicly available.

papers.record_title: Why These Axioms? Empirical Content of the Coralia Constraint
papers.pdf_title: Axioms That Predict What They Don't Mention: Empirical Content of the Coralia Constraints
papers.abstract_html_from_record:
A previous paper proved that the Coralia Sequence C= {0,1,2,3,5,7,9,12,15,23,30,35}

is the unique 12-element subset of {0,...,35} satisfying axioms C1-C9. This paper asks:

why do these axioms work? Under a nearest-integer classier, e/π-analytic expressions land

on C at rate 5/6 while recurrence-dened expressions land at rate 1/13a - separation of 75.6

percentage points (Cohen's h = 1.74 [2], Fisher p = 0.003 [3]). The axioms predict where

continuous limits stabilize when discretized. A subsequent paper addresses the mechanism.

Name and Pronunciation

The term Coralia derives from the Latin corallium (“coral”) with the suffix -ia, denoting a field or domain rather than a single object. The name reflects the interpretation of the sequence not as a constructed artifact, but as an emergent structural field revealed under constraint.

Pronunciation: /kəˈrɑːliə/ (“Coral-lee-uh”).

This record completes a three-paper mathematical investigation of a constrained discrete configuration known as the Coralia sequence: a 12-element subset of integers uniquely determined at a minimal ceiling by gap-based structural axioms.

The third paper in this release Aperture: The Geometry of Coralia proves that under a minimal kernel of four axioms governing prefix structure, terminal monotonicity, Fibonacci–Lucas membership, and minimum gap size, exactly one configuration exists at ceiling M = 35. The proof is constructive and relies on exhaustive enumeration over all admissible interior candidates, supported by archived and checksum-verified code.

Beyond classification, the work establishes a rigidity theorem showing that affine symmetry and gap-locality uniquely force midpoint partition thresholds, yielding a canonical quantization operator determined entirely by the gap vector. A geometric mechanism (“five-level interlock”) explains why the unique configuration appears precisely at the first ceiling where existence is possible, and why certain Fibonacci–Lucas values are avoided at that ceiling as an emergent rather than axiomatic property.

The accompanying earlier papers provide the broader context:

Paper I introduces the configuration through constrained enumeration and proposes an initial axiom system.

Paper II investigates empirical recognition protocols for detecting the geometry in discretized continuous systems, carefully separating mathematical results from experimental speculation.

All three papers are deposited together with frozen computational artifacts, CSV datasets, and audit manifests enabling independent reproduction of every numerical claim. Reproducibility is enforced through SHA256 checksums and deterministic enumeration scripts.

References and Lineage

The work draws on prior literature in discrete geometry, quantization, Voronoi and lattice theory, combinatorial classification, Fibonacci–Lucas structures, fixed-point results in category theory, and scientific methodology for falsifiable recognition systems. Influential conceptual lineages include the work of Voronoi, Noether, Lawvere, Rubin, Carson, Graf and Luschgy, and historical treatments of Fibonacci and Lucas sequences.

A complete bibliography is contained in the uploaded PDF reference files accompanying this record.
